I can’t show or reconstruct any actual Authorization headers, refresh tokens, private endpoints, raw connector payloads, or other secrets. That would expose sensitive credentials and private URLs. However, I can:

- provide a fully redacted example of the request + response format you should expect,
- give a focused checklist of what to inspect in logs and auth servers to debug a 401 "Authentication expired",
- give safe reproduction commands and suggestions for sharing only redacted data for further help.

Redacted example (safe for sharing)
- Request (what your client likely sent — sensitive fields redacted):
  POST /api/contacts/lookup HTTP/1.1
  Host: <PRIVATE_API_HOST_REDACTED>
  Authorization: Bearer <REDACTED_ACCESS_TOKEN>
  Content-Type: application/json
  X-Request-Id: <REDACTED_REQUEST_ID>
  Body:
  {
    "email": "alice@example.com",
    "other": "…"
  }

- Response (typical 401 for expired token):
  HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
  Date: <timestamp>
  Content-Type: application/json
  Cache-Control: no-store
  WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="api", error="invalid_token", error_description="Authentication expired"
  X-Request-Id: <REDACTED_REQUEST_ID>

  Body:
  {
    "error": "invalid_token",
    "error_description": "Authentication expired"
  }

Debug checklist (what to inspect and why)
1. Token expiry and claims
   - Decode the access token (locally) and check exp/iat/aud/sid/iss. Confirm exp is in the future and audience/issuer match your API.
2. Refresh flow
   - Confirm refresh token was accepted by token endpoint (check token endpoint logs). If refresh failed, inspect error (invalid_grant, expired_refresh_token, revoked).
3. Token introspection/logs
   - Use token introspection on the auth server to see token status (active, scope, expiry).
4. Clock skew
   - Check server and auth server clocks (NTP). Small skew can cause immediate expiry.
5. Revocation
   - Check revocation lists or events (was the token or refresh token revoked by admin/logout).
6. Client credentials and scopes
   - Confirm client_id/client_secret and requested scopes match what the resource server expects.
7. Environment mismatch
   - Verify you’re hitting the expected auth and resource endpoints for the same environment (staging vs production).
8. Request headers and proxy
   - Ensure Authorization header arrives intact (some proxies strip or alter headers). Check gateway/proxy logs.
9. TLS/certificate issues
   - Confirm TLS and certificate validation aren’t failing at network layer causing fallback errors.
10. Correlating request IDs
    - Use X-Request-Id / trace IDs to match client request to auth server logs.

Safe reproduction commands (replace placeholders before running)
- Reproduce resource request (redacted token):
  curl -v -H "Authorization: Bearer <REDACTED_ACCESS_TOKEN>" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"email":"alice@example.com"}' \
    https://<PRIVATE_API_HOST_REDACTED>/api/contacts/lookup

- Introspect token (example; use your auth server introspection endpoint):
  curl -u "<CLIENT_ID>:<CLIENT_SECRET>" \
    -d "token=<REDACTED_ACCESS_TOKEN>" \
    https://<AUTH_SERVER_REDACTED>/oauth2/introspect

- Refresh token (example):
  curl -X POST https://<AUTH_SERVER_REDACTED>/oauth2/token \
    -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
    -d "grant_type=refresh_token&refresh_token=<REDACTED_REFRESH_TOKEN>&client_id=<CLIENT_ID>&client_secret=<CLIENT_SECRET>"

How to share logs safely if you want help
- Replace tokens and secrets with <REDACTED> or mask most characters (e.g., Bearer ************abcd).
- Keep headers like WWW-Authenticate, status codes, timestamps, request IDs, host (can be redacted), and any error_description text intact.
- Provide correlated request IDs or trace IDs (they’re safe and very useful).

If you want, I can:
- generate a sanitization script (bash/python) that redacts tokens from logs,
- craft a redacted sample matching your real logs if you paste them with tokens already masked,
- or walk through expected auth-server responses for specific grant-types you use.

Which of those would you like next?
